title: Waiting in line
hookLine: The Buddha remembers sitting as a boy in a rose-apple tree's shade, and finds the way
tomorrow: what did an emperor tell himself in the morning about rude people?

lines: A BOY IN THE ROSE-APPLE SHADE.
cards: The pharmacy line hasn't moved in ages. Everyone's staring at a phone. The Buddha told a story about himself that starts somewhere like this, in a stuck place.
Before his awakening he had been starving himself, trying to force a breakthrough, and it wasn't coming. Then a memory surfaced.

As a boy, while his father was busy at work, he had sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, and a quiet, happy stillness had come over him all on its own. Nobody asked anything of him. He was just sitting.
Could that, he wondered, be the way?

teach.b: In the Pali Canon he tells what came next: with the memory came a knowing, that is the way.
Then he asked himself why he was afraid of that kind of happiness, one that has nothing to do with craving, and decided he wasn't. He ate again and stopped the war with his own body.
Buddhists call the path that followed the middle way, between indulging and grinding.
And some teachers link that stillness in the shade to a practice he later taught, anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing: breathing in, knowing you breathe in; breathing out, knowing you breathe out.
A queue is a little rose-apple shade. Nothing's being asked of you but to wait, and the breath is right there. Not forcing calm.
Not scrolling to escape. Just in, and knowing it. Out, and knowing it.
This path borrows that practice, with its source named, for every line you'll ever stand in.

how: Buddhists practice anapanasati, knowing each breath as it comes in and goes out; people on this path borrow it for lines and waits, standing quietly instead of scrolling.

o: a polite rule about who gets served first
a sign of poor planning that wastes your day
a plain wait you can turn into breathing practice

games.q: the shade and the breath: tap the pairs.
p: what he knew when the memory came

s: the Buddha's breakthrough came from forcing himself harder
it came after he remembered an effortless stillness in the shade, and ate again.
the Buddha asked himself why he was afraid of that kind of happiness
a happiness with nothing to do with craving. he decided not to fear it.
mindful breathing means making every breath slow and deep
the popular version. the teaching is knowing: breathing in, you know you're breathing in.

games.q: your coworker says waiting is wasted time, so she answers emails in every line. what fits the rose-apple shade?
o: a wait can be the shade: nothing asked of you but to breathe and know it.
she's right: the Buddha taught never to let a single minute go to waste.
lines are too noisy; real breathing practice only works in silence at home.
games.why: the Buddha's way opened when he remembered a boy just waiting in the shade. the breath practice he taught asks only that you know each breath.

practice: Stand up if you can, the way you'd stand in a line: weight on both feet, hands loose. Breathe in, and know you're breathing in. Breathe out, and know you're breathing out, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Waiting in line: a plain wait where the boy's shade comes back. Breathing in, knowing it; breathing out, knowing it.

orig.note: Pali, written in Devanagari: mindfulness of breathing in and out.

carryVoice: Your line: the queue, a little shade to breathe in. Two of fourteen, and a week of lines gathered.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 36, Mahasaccaka Sutta (the memory of the rose-apple shade; 'that is the way'; not afraid of that happiness; taking food again)
Majjhima Nikaya 118, Anapanasati Sutta (breathing in, one knows one breathes in)
